To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the DNA glycosyles Ogg1 and/or Nth1 do not contribute to class switching in activated mouse splenic B cells.
the DNA glycosyles Ogg1 and/or Nth1 do not contribute to Ig class switch recombination or to c-myc recombination in activated B cells.
the absence of Ogg1 and/or Nth1 does not alter the levels of DSBs in splenic B cell nuclei, or the efficiency of Ig class switch recombination in splenic B lymphocytes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the enzymes Ogg1 andNth1 in the generation of DNA breaks in activated splenic B cells.
the effect of deletion on the DNA glycosyles Ogg1 and/or Nth1 on DNA breaks and class switching in activated splenic B cells.
DNA damage and repair during B cell class switching and the possible role of DNA repair in this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Ogg1 and/or Nth1 do not contribute to the formation of S region DSBs or to class switching in activated B cells.
Ogg1 and/or Nth1 do not contribute to class switching.
these DNA glycosylase enzymes do not contribute significantly to class switching or c-myc recombination in B cells in vivo.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the DNA glycosylation pathway for oxidized bases in the IgH locus does not play a significant role in class switching.
Ogg1 and/or Nth1 do not contribute to the DNA damage that occurs during B cell activation and class switching.
Ogg1 and/or Nth1 do not appear to contribute to class switching or to c-myc DNBs in activated splenic B cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the DNA repair enzymes Ogg1 and/or Nth1 do not play an essential role in Ig class switching.
Ogg1 and/or Nth1 do not appear to be important for class switching and c-myc recombination in B cells.
the DNA glycosylation repair pathway for oxidized bases does not appear to play an important role in class switching.
